text: {"answer":"The evidence is mixed rather than uniform. A randomised call centre experiment found a 13 percent increase in completed calls among remote staff, attributed to a quieter environment and fewer breaks [remote_work#0]. Output per engineer measured by completed tickets held steady or improved after full transitions to distributed work in several large technology firms [remote_work#3]. Remote arrangements also reduce attrition, and lower turnover limits productivity losses from repeated hiring and retraining [remote_work#2]. Against this, a large field experiment found remote data entry workers were 18 percent less productive than office counterparts on identical tasks [remote_work#6]. Studies of software teams report slower onboarding and weaker mentoring for juniors, which can depress team output over time [remote_work#4]. Communication also becomes more siloed after a remote transition [remote_work#5]. Self-reported productivity gains often fail to appear in objective output measures [remote_work#7], so self-report evidence should be discounted.","confidence":40,"one_line":"Remote work's productivity effect is mixed: gains in some call-centre and engineering settings, losses in data entry and team mentoring."}
